paragraphs: A further difficulty appears when the city tries to define the procedure by which future changes will be approved. Requiring unanimous consent might seem to protect the public character of the square, yet it could enable a small group to block uses that later residents had good reason to want. Allowing a simple majority to authorize any alteration would avoid that obstacle while exposing less powerful users to decisions made without serious attention to their needs. A procedure cannot be assessed merely by asking whether it permits change; the distribution of the power to initiate, resist and review a change matters as well.

The city might therefore preserve records of why particular protections were adopted, while making their application open to later criticism. Such records would not instruct future residents to share present preferences. They would enable a later generation to distinguish a restriction designed to keep the space public from one that happened to preserve a currently fashionable arrangement. Even that distinction would remain contestable: what counts as a public use may itself change. The purpose of transmitting reasons would be to make revision answerable to an intelligible history, not to turn that history into a final authority against which no new reason could count.

There is also a material condition which a discussion of procedures can conceal. A formal right to propose a change gives little practical capacity to people who lack the time, information or resources needed to use it. Maintaining collective choice may therefore require support for participation as well as a rule about who may vote. None of this allows present residents to certify that their arrangements will be endorsed in fifty years. It offers a more limited basis for responsibility: they can explain which powers they are preserving and why, acknowledge whose interests they may have failed to anticipate, and leave later users means of revising both the arrangement and the explanation. A commitment to future freedom would then include a commitment to being questioned. Preserving a question would thus involve preserving people's ability to demand reasons, not merely leaving the furniture easy to move.

paragraphs: Suppose the minutes are checked by the speaker, who approves the wording because she remembers the conditions under which the discussion occurred. Her approval may correct some errors without ensuring that an absent reader can reconstruct those conditions. The document's adequacy cannot therefore be settled simply by asking whether the original participants recognize their own words in it. Recognition from within a shared context and interpretation outside it place different demands on the same record.

An editor preparing a short public summary might attach a note stating that the proposal remains subject to the two conditions. If the conditions themselves are unavailable, however, the note must not create the impression that their content has been verified. A responsible summary can mark an unresolved dependency without pretending to supply what is missing. That is different from using a vague expression of caution to conceal the fact that nobody has checked which limit the caution was meant to preserve.

This distinction becomes especially important when one summary is quoted in another. Each writer may reproduce the sentence received accurately, while the chain progressively detaches it from the circumstances that made it a conditional claim. Assigning all responsibility to the interpreter at the first meeting would overlook the later choices through which a provisional recommendation became a public commitment. Yet spreading responsibility across a chain should not make it disappear: each stage can be asked what a reader needs in order not to mistake the kind of claim being transmitted.

The aim is not to prevent a document from travelling beyond the conversation that produced it. That travel is often the reason a record is made. It is to carry forward enough of the relevant qualifications for the claim to remain assessable in a new setting. A shorter text may consequently be less faithful than a slightly longer one, not because length is a measure of accuracy, but because the relation between words and commitments is itself part of what an accurate account must preserve. A reader should be able to tell whether a limit was verified, reported from memory or left unresolved.

paragraphs: The proposed forum could nevertheless become another ceremony if its regular occurrence were treated as proof that the obligation had been met. A town might advertise the number of meetings held while leaving repeated requests unanswered. Conversely, a forum that produced no immediate agreement could still reveal a continuing effect which the town had previously failed to acknowledge. Neither the visibility of discussion nor the absence of consensus would, by itself, show whether the institution was responding adequately. The relevant question would concern what happened to the claims after they had been heard.

One way to make that question answerable would be to keep a public record of requests, responses and reasons for delay. A refusal could then be distinguished from a request that had silently fallen out of consideration, without assuming that every refusal was unjust. Those affected would also need a way to challenge the reasons offered, rather than merely confirm that an official had replied. Such arrangements would not settle how much material repair was owed, but they could prevent the existence of a listening process from becoming evidence that no further response was required. An institution can formally receive a complaint while remaining practically closed to what the complaint asks it to reconsider.

There would still be disagreement about which present effects could reasonably be attributed to the earlier policy. Public recognition should not exempt those claims from examination, any more than uncertainty about a particular claim should erase recognition of the wrong already acknowledged. Keeping these judgements separate would allow the town to investigate responsibilities without making the monument's legitimacy depend on accepting every later demand. The monument could retain its significance as a correction to silence while ceasing to function as a certificate of completed repair. What matters is not whether the apology can be expressed once and for all, but whether the public act makes continuing questions harder to ignore rather than easier to declare finished. Its continuing role would be tested by whether a new request could receive an explained response, not by whether another anniversary attracted a larger audience.

paragraphs: Imagine that members agree to share some additional costs across the whole scheme rather than charge them only to the predicted high-need group. The forecast may be useful in estimating the resources required, even though it no longer determines which group pays the difference. A defender of the model need not regard this decision as a rejection of evidence. The same prediction can inform more than one distribution, because an estimate of likely expenditure does not contain a principle specifying whose responsibility that expenditure should become.

This leaves an important objection: a shared contribution may itself impose burdens on people whose resources are limited. To acknowledge that difficulty is not to return automatically to the rule that each category must finance its predicted costs. It is to recognize that both arrangements require justification in terms of the relationships the scheme is meant to sustain. The relevant comparison concerns the effects and reasons of competing rules, not a choice between a rule grounded in facts and an alternative grounded in no facts at all.

Nor does the distinction imply that better prediction is politically unimportant. A revised estimate could show that an arrangement previously believed affordable would require resources the members cannot provide. Such information changes the options available without, by itself, selecting the fairest option among those that remain. Evidence can constrain a judgement without supplying the whole judgement.

The model's designers should therefore be able to explain what their categories predict and which decisions lie outside that prediction. If a contribution rule is presented as though it simply follows from the data, members may lose the opportunity to question a moral choice precisely because it has been described in technical language. More detailed personal information would not repair that omission unless the missing principle of distribution were also made explicit.

An institution that separates these tasks can take accuracy seriously while permitting argument about solidarity, responsibility and resources. It does not promise a method by which all such arguments will reach agreement. It makes it possible to locate a disagreement where it belongs, instead of asking a model to answer a question whose terms it was never designed to decide.

paragraphs: A new assessment would first have to separate confidence from accuracy. An editor who works slowly and expresses doubt may still identify an error that a confident colleague misses; a fluent independent translation may also be wrong. The earlier test could raise a question about a change in capacity without establishing which element of performance had changed or what caused the change. Comparing work before and after automation would require attention to the difficulty of the material and to differences in the people tested, not merely to the presence or absence of the system.

The team might then examine cases in which a draft is persuasive but rests on a mistaken interpretation. Success would depend partly on recognizing when the suggestion needed to be checked independently. A test that announces in advance that every example contains an error could measure correction while giving away the very judgement whose survival matters in ordinary work. Conversely, an exercise consisting only of exceptional failures might say little about the resources needed to maintain reliable routine production. Both the selection of cases and the information given to editors would shape what could reasonably be inferred from their results.

Training could consequently preserve selected forms of independent work without attempting to recreate the entire former workflow. Time spent on such practice would need to be justified by the role it played in checking and recovering from failures, rather than by the fact that the activity had once occupied most of the day. The same scrutiny should apply to the new skill of evaluating suggestions: calling it a skill would not establish that every editor had acquired it equally well, or that it would remain adequate as the system changed. A new division of labour could create capacities as well as dependencies, both of which required evidence rather than celebration or regret alone.

The managers would therefore need an account of what level of independent judgement the organization intended to retain, how it would notice a decline and what response that decline would warrant. That account could be revised as the work changed, but revision should not make each observed result automatically acceptable. An apparently successful process may deserve confidence partly because people remain able to identify circumstances in which they should withdraw it. The purpose of assessment is then neither to prove that automation has destroyed expertise nor to certify that improved output has made independent understanding unnecessary. It is to examine whether the organization retains the means to discover where its present success stops.
